prize_parts.citation: For showing how firm heterogeneity and selection into exporting shape international trade, productivity and the gains from trade.

statement.case_for: My laureate configuration is unchanged: B020 with Melitz and Helpman. What changed is how I weigh B001, and my second alternative. The case is that firm heterogeneity and selection moved trade analysis from industries and countries to firms. It explains who exports, who invests abroad and how openness reallocates resources, and it produced predictions that firm-level and transaction-level data could confront. Those predictions have been examined for more than two decades across many countries and datasets. The framework also changed empirical practice and quantitative policy evaluation, and it spread to industrial organisation and macro. On the Chair's question, I do not think the omission of Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum from the credited list is disqualifying. Melitz (2003) is the conceptual model of selection, and Helpman, Melitz and Yeaple (2004) is its natural extension to exporting versus FDI. A citation worded around the mechanism, and a Scientific Background that sets out the empirical precursors, would be accurate without implying the firm-level literature is exhausted. I would not add Redding, whose quantitative and spatial work is later and builds on an established framework. If the Committee recognises trade, I could accept B001 as a single-part award, and it is my first alternative. I would not combine the two Helpman strands. If forced to a choice, I would recognise him for the firm-heterogeneity work, because I judge that contribution to have had the wider effect on measurement and on cross-field spillovers.
statement.case_against: The attribution boundary remains the main weakness. A Melitz-Helpman award leaves out the empirical and quantitative originators, and I cannot repair that by adding uncredited names. Some welfare conclusions depend on parametric assumptions such as Pareto productivity and CES demand, so the quantitative gains-from-trade claims are less secure than the qualitative selection and reallocation mechanism. Helpman's overlap with B001 means the Committee is choosing between two distinct achievements, and reasonable members can weight empirical footprint against attribution cleanliness differently. I also ranked B001 eighth at the opening. After Hjalmarsson's and Teorell's responses I think that placed too much weight on mixed test results. B001 is a serious rival whose standing rests on framework influence, and it has the cleaner credit. My preference for B020 is a judgement about empirical traction and spillover, held with moderate confidence. It is not a claim that B001 is scientifically weak. Finally, B020 has no majority support in the round-1 written positions, and I do not treat that count as evidence of merit either way.

responses.point: Hjalmarsson asks me to separate 'contested magnitudes' from 'no lasting contribution' for B001. She argues that Grossman and Helpman gave empiricists a structural equation to estimate, and that mixed estimates are the normal outcome for a model with testable implications.
responses.response: I accept this distinction, and it moves me. The influence of protection for sale does not depend on every estimate confirming it, and my eighth-place opening rank overstated the penalty for mixed results. The framework did organise a structural empirical literature on trade policy. I still hold that the question for a single prize is which contribution changed what economists measure and how they evaluate policy, and I think firm heterogeneity did that more broadly. For me the gap is one of degree and not of kind. That is why B001 is now my first alternative and a configuration I could accept.

responses.point: Teorell holds B001 first and says the B020 attribution gap (Bernard, Eaton, Jensen, Kortum) invites a priority dispute that the Grossman-Helpman pairing avoids. He would want a clear argument for why Melitz and Helpman, rather than a wider group, define the contribution.
responses.response: That is a fair challenge, and I will answer it directly. The credited-list problem is real, but a prize is awarded for a discovery and not for every contributor to a literature. The discovery here is the selection mechanism, in which productivity heterogeneity and fixed export costs determine who exports. Melitz's model states it, and Helpman, Melitz and Yeaple extend it to the choice between exporting and FDI. The empirical firm-level facts motivated and then tested it. A citation on the mechanism makes that division clear. I agree this is a judgement and that B001 has the lower priority-dispute risk. I weigh that risk as manageable and as smaller than the difference in empirical reach. I also agree with you that B001 should stand on its own case, not on Helpman's credit under B020.

responses.point: Hassler, as chair, says he did not rank B020 at the opening but takes the argument seriously. He wants the case for B020 stated against B001 directly, and he stresses that the choice should not treat Helpman as a bridge that makes either route easier. He prefers B016, whose breadth he contrasts with B001's single framework.
responses.response: Stated against B001 directly: B020 has the wider empirical footprint, with selection and reallocation predictions checked in many firm-level datasets, and it spread into IO and quantitative macro. B001 has the cleaner two-person credit and no maturity concern, but its central prediction has been confirmed less consistently. Neither case depends on Helpman as a bridge, and I agree they should be judged as separate achievements. I also declare my own tie to you. We co-authored a 2026 paper with Ellingsen, and I am not treating that as a reason to weight your view on B016. On B016, I accept that it is a broad programme. Its weaker identification and its overlap with the 2024 prize are the reasons I keep it out of my alternatives, and my ranking of B016 should not be read as a judgement on its scientific standing.

responses.point: Andersson says that unresolved credit for Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum and the parametric dependence of some welfare results make him cautious about whether B020 can support a clean, defensible citation today. He would want that boundary settled before ranking it above B001. He also describes my own attribution analysis as pointing against B020.
responses.response: I agree the boundary cannot be repaired by adding names, and the ballot entry limits what we can do. I read it differently, though. A credit gap that I can state precisely, and that a mechanism-focused citation and background document can handle, is a manageable risk. It is not a reason to prefer a candidate whose empirical record is weaker. On parametric dependence, the qualitative selection and reallocation results are more robust than the size of the welfare gains, and the citation should speak to the mechanism and not to a point estimate of gains. I accept that your reading of the same facts leads to B001, and I treat this as a real difference in weighting. It is not a difference over the facts.

uncertainties: Whether the credit boundary with Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum is close enough to the core that a Melitz-Helpman award would be seen as incomplete, and whether a mechanism-centred citation resolves it.

Whether the Committee prefers to recognise Helpman through B020 or B001. I would not combine the two, and I am unsure how the Committee will weigh breadth of written support against my empirical-footprint argument.
How robust the welfare-gains results are to parametric assumptions on productivity distributions and demand.
How much weight the mixed empirical record of protection for sale should carry. I now weigh it less than I did at the opening, but I still weigh it.
Whether the 2022 prize leaves enough marginal case for B031 to compete, if the Committee does not choose trade.
My assessments of priority and attribution rest on memory and the colleagues' written positions. I have not independently verified them.
statement.conflict_note: No candidate-specific connection is apparent from the supplied profile. My research in industrial organisation and international trade (pricing, exchange-rate pass-through, invoicing currency) is thematically close to B020 and B001, and to the IO candidate B041. I judge them on the common criteria. I co-authored a 2026 paper with committee chair John Hassler and former chair Tore Ellingsen. Neither is a candidate. Hassler prefers B016, and I do not treat his position or our collaboration as evidence for or against any candidate. My spouse's public political role is noted as a public fact only, and nothing in the profile suggests it bears on any shortlisted candidate. I disclose these ties and do not adjudicate them.
